Closes ethos-i1z8, ethos-21v0.

## `ethos mission result` accepted YAML-comment-truncated values

Found for real on PR #516: an evidence entry written

    - name: PR #515 merged as 6f61406 — 6/6 CI checks green, ...

parsed as `name: PR`, because YAML treats an unquoted ` #` as a comment.
Validation only required a non-empty name, so it passed, persisted, and
round-tripped through `mission close` with `status: pass` intact — a
record asserting success about something it no longer described.

Detected by mechanism, not heuristic: yaml.v3 returns the discarded text
as the node's LineComment, so a truncated scalar is exactly one that is
plain and carries one. Quoted and block scalars are excluded by style; a
length rule would reject `make check` and miss a long value cut at
character 40.

Membership follows one rule: a field is checked when its grammar admits
whitespace. Handles, enums, mission IDs, timestamps, and numbers cannot
contain " #", which is why the scaffolds may keep annotating those. Free
text and paths both qualify.

Review corrected the first attempt substantially. The scope had named
`delegations[].message`, which does not exist — DelegationTemplate has
no such field, so the guard protected nothing while
`preconditions[].message` went unguarded. Three reviewers caught it
independently, and the CHANGELOG repeated the same false claim. Applying
the whitespace rule systematically then found fields no review flagged:
write_set[], extract_into[], inputs.files[], inputs.references[],
preconditions[].require_read[], inputs.trigger.subject, and
delegations[].spawn_pattern.

Also closed: paths were wrongly treated as constrained (validateWriteSet
Entry permits spaces and #, so `path: reports/PR #515.txt` persisted
`reports/PR`), and YAML aliases bypassed the walk entirely — an anchored
truncated scalar reached a checked field as an AliasNode with no scalar
to inspect. Aliases are now refused outright rather than resolved: a
mission artifact needing alias resolution to read is a poor audit
record, and a resolver subtly wrong about nested merges reopens the
bypass while looking closed.

Guarded against recurrence by reflection: every scope entry must resolve
against the Go type, so a scope naming a nonexistent field now fails the
build. That check is load-bearing because Inputs.UnmarshalYAML decodes
without KnownFields, so a decoder-only probe would let a typo parse.

The scaffolds now quote their two path values — ethos would otherwise
have rejected its own output, and the scaffold now demonstrates the
remedy the error message prescribes.

Two findings rejected after being disproven, both pinned by tests since
each was independently suspected: `prose: # comment` (yaml.v3 attaches a
valueless key's comment to the key node) and empty sequence items
(`- # note` leaves LineComment empty and displaces the text to the next
item's HeadComment, which the check never reads).

## `internal/repomiss` had no tests

97 lines, zero test files, no `ok` line — while being the leaf type
shared by the four layered stores and internal/vendor + internal/doctor.
Now 100.0%, repomiss.go unchanged. Sorted's copy property is pinned
twice and its stability claim proved across all six permutations.

## Verification

Every guard falsified, not merely observed green. The MCP call site was
mutated to a no-op to confirm the new handler test is what goes red
while the other 28 packages stay green; both CLI sites verified the same
way. `make check` with -race: 29 ok, 0 FAIL (up from 28).

The line I wrote was:

Detection is by mechanism, not heuristic: yaml.v3 hands back the discarded
text as the node's LineComment, so a truncated scalar is exactly one that is
plain and carries one. Quoted and block scalars are excluded by style. A
length rule would have rejected "make check" and missed a long value cut at
character 40.

Membership follows one rule: a field is checked when its grammar admits
whitespace. Handles, enums, mission IDs, timestamps and numbers cannot
contain " #", which is why the scaffolds may keep annotating those. Free
text and paths both qualify.

Applied across all four submitted-artifact schemas — results, reflections,
corrections, and contracts. Corrections were the sharpest case and were not
on my original list: the artifact that retracts a false claim about a PR
would itself have been cut at that PR's number.

My first attempt was substantially wrong, and three reviewers caught the
same thing independently. The contract scope named delegations[].message —
a field that does not exist. DelegationTemplate has role, spawn_pattern,

and delegations[].spawn_pattern — the field that actually exists where I had
been pointing at a phantom.

(validateWriteSetEntry permits spaces and #, so `path: reports/PR #515.txt`
persisted as `reports/PR`), and YAML aliases bypassed the walk entirely.

WHAT WAS BROKEN

Ethos answered "which Claude Code session is calling me?" by walking the
process tree to the topmost `claude` ancestor and caching the result for the
process lifetime. That ancestor is not per-session — it is `claude daemon
run`, one process shared by every concurrent Claude Code session on the host.
Its PID keyed a single-valued pointer file, so every session's SessionStart
overwrote the same file and the last writer won.

The consequence is the part that matters: this was a silent WRONG answer, not
a silent absence. A commit in one repo could carry another repo's Mission: and
Delegation: trailers. DES-054's audit chain did not merely go missing — it
could lie. For a product whose value is the audit trail, that is the worst
available failure mode.

MEASURED, NOT THEORISED

Six distinct session rosters on one host all listed participant 518779,
spanning four repos and served by three pointer files. Running `ethos session`
from punt-labs/ethos reported `Repo: punt-labs/z-spec`. Hours later the same
command from the same repo answered punt-labs/agentsmesh — a third repo —
because another session had started and overwritten the pointer in between.

THE FIX

Session identity is declared by the harness and read per call: never inferred
from the process tree, never cached.

- Key on CLAUDE_PID, the owning process's own PID, which Claude Code sets on
  every spawned subprocess. Distinct per session, unlike the shared topmost
  ancestor. The tree walk remains as a fallback for headless, CI, SDK, and
  older Claude Code.
- Corroborate before trusting it. CLAUDE_PID is captured once at spawn and
  never re-observed, so a dead ancestor's recycled PID would otherwise resolve
  to a real, live, wrong process.

FOLLOW-ON

This opened what became cluster 1 — the remaining session-identity defects
closed in PR #507, including the commit-msg hook header that described the
opposite of what its code did on the branch where the misattribution entered.
